blocks.text: Born in 1954 in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, Cindy Sherman has built one of the most influential bodies of work in contemporary art by photographing herself without ever making self-portraits. A student at Buffalo State College, she turned from painting to photography, and in 1977, newly settled in New York, she began the “Untitled Film Stills,” 70 black-and-white images in which she posed as anonymous heroines of imaginary films. The series made her a central figure of the Pictures Generation. Working alone in her studio as model, makeup artist, costume designer and photographer, she has since used wigs, prosthetics and, later, digital tools to dissect the stereotypes of gender, age and class circulated by cinema, advertising and art history. Her work has been the subject of major retrospectives, including at the Museum of Modern Art in 2012 and at the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris in 2020.

This segment comes from “Transformation,” an episode of the fifth season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in October 2009. It surveys some thirty years of Sherman’s untitled works, grouped into informally named series such as fairy tales, centerfolds, history portraits, Hollywood/Hampton types and clowns.
